name: Vantage Data Centers

profile.reading:
Per Vantage Data Centers' own facility page, this campus is located at 45 S Bullard Avenue, Goodyear, AZ 85338; Vantage markets the campus as "Phoenix," though the confirmed address places it in Goodyear, a separate West Valley suburb. Vantage describes the campus as 50 acres with more than 1 million square feet at full buildout, five data centers planned, and 176 megawatts of critical IT load, delivered via a 69-plus kilovolt incoming feed distributed at 12kV and 480V with N+1 power redundancy (mechanical N+2 planned). Two buildings, AZ11 and AZ12, are individually cited on the page as each achieving Green Globe for New Construction certification from the Green Building Initiative; a third building, AZ13, is confirmed to exist by third-party trackers but is not individually named on Vantage's own page.

Vantage is a private, Denver, Colorado-headquartered operator; DigitalBridge acquired the company in March 2017, and in January 2024 Vantage announced a $6.4 billion equity investment round led by DigitalBridge and Silver Lake. Phoenix-area utilities have faced sustained strain from data center growth: Arizona Public Service has said it received 19 gigawatts of electrical service requests from data centers and large commercial users it currently cannot serve, with individual requests now averaging about 500 megawatts each; APS filed for a nearly 14% residential rate increase expected no earlier than July 2026, and SRP raised rates in November 2025, including a 50% increase in fixed monthly charges for single-family homes.

Arizona's West Valley, including Goodyear, has become one of the fastest-growing U.S. data center corridors alongside Mesa, Phoenix, and Chandler, drawing Vantage alongside Meta, Google, Microsoft, and EdgeConneX. Arizona Public Service and Salt River Project have both signed large-load interconnection agreements with data center developers in the West Valley, and APS has periodically flagged transmission capacity constraints in Buckeye and Goodyear as a factor pacing new project timelines. Water use is a live regulatory issue in the Phoenix metro generally, since Arizona's Department of Water Resources designates the area an Active Management Area with assured-supply requirements, and large air-cooled or hybrid-cooled data centers have drawn attention from Goodyear city council and state legislators weighing the tradeoff between data center tax revenue, jobs, and long-term aquifer strain in a desert climate.

profile.reading:
Per Vantage Data Centers' own facility page, this campus, Santa Clara CA2, is located at 737 Mathew Street, Santa Clara, CA 95051. Vantage describes the 9-acre campus as three four-story data centers totaling 541,000 square feet and 75 megawatts of critical IT load, powered through three 50-megawatt on-site transformers with 415/240V distribution and N+1 redundancy; cooling uses closed-loop chilled water with water-side economizers, also N+1. No certifications (LEED, Uptime Tier) or opening year are stated on the page.

Vantage is a private, Denver, Colorado-headquartered operator; DigitalBridge acquired the company in March 2017, and in January 2024 Vantage announced a $6.4 billion equity investment round led by DigitalBridge and Silver Lake. California regulators are actively reworking how large data center loads are billed and interconnected as demand grows statewide, directly relevant to Santa Clara's dense colocation submarket. Under SB 57 (2025), the California Public Utilities Commission opened a rate-design rulemaking in April 2026 addressing electric rate impacts of data centers and other large transmission-connected loads; the California Independent System Operator separately published a formal issue paper on large-load interconnection considerations in January 2026.

Santa Clara sits at the center of Silicon Valley's data center market, one of the most supply-constrained in the country because Santa Clara's municipal utility, Silicon Valley Power, has at times paused new large-load interconnections while it builds additional substation capacity, a constraint that has pushed some hyperscale and colocation growth toward Santa Clara's edges and neighboring cities. California's Title 24 energy code and statewide water-efficiency rules shape cooling-system design for new Silicon Valley data centers, and the City of Santa Clara has periodically debated its own data center power-allocation policy given competing demand from other large commercial and residential development in the same substation service areas. Vantage's Santa Clara presence sits among a dense cluster of competing operators, including Digital Realty, Equinix, and CoreSite, within a few miles of this site.

Vantage describes the roughly 12-acre (5-hectare) campus as two four-story buildings totaling 390,000 square feet (36,000 square meters) and 48 megawatts of critical IT load, at an average density of 300 watts per square foot (3.23 kW per square meter), delivered via 480V distribution with N+1 redundancy and stated as 100% concurrently maintainable. Vantage is a private, Denver, Colorado-headquartered operator with a substantial international footprint across EMEA and APAC in addition to North America; DigitalBridge acquired the company in March 2017, and in January 2024 Vantage announced a $6.4 billion equity investment round led by DigitalBridge and Silver Lake, with Colony Capital, AustralianSuper, GIC, and ADIA cited among its other investors. Warsaw is Poland's largest and most established data center market, drawing hyperscale and colocation investment as Central and Eastern Europe's cloud infrastructure hub, distinct from the US-centric markets tracked elsewhere in this registry.

Warsaw has emerged as a significant Central European data center hub as cloud providers and colocation operators seek EU-jurisdiction capacity outside the traditional FLAP-D markets of Frankfurt, London, Amsterdam, Paris, and Dublin. Poland's data center growth has been supported by Warsaw's position as a national and regional connectivity hub, EU data-residency requirements that have pushed some multinational customers toward in-country capacity, and Poland's power grid operator PSE's ongoing transmission investment as large digital-infrastructure loads grow alongside the country's broader industrial electricity demand. Vantage entered the Warsaw market as part of a broader European expansion that has also included Berlin and other EU metros, positioning WAW1 to serve both domestic Polish enterprise and financial-sector customers and multinational cloud and colocation tenants seeking EU-based capacity.

Vantage does not publish this campus on its own site at all, so this entry relies on secondary sourcing: Data Center Dynamics reporting on the building permit. TX21 covers approximately 360,000 square feet across three stories, at a stated construction cost of roughly $157 million; its permit was originally filed for a December 2023 to June 2025 timeline, but the launch date appears to have slipped and is unclear as of this research. No power/MW figure is disclosed in any source found, and no certifications are published, consistent with the building's incomplete status.

Vantage acquired 31 acres at State Highway 151/Wiseman Boulevard in August 2023 for its Westover Hills sub-campus, home to TX21 and TX22, separate from the Texas Research Park sub-campus (Omicron Drive, home to TX11 and TX12). This San Antonio campus is distinct from Vantage's much larger "Frontier" mega-campus, a separate $25 billion, 1.4-gigawatt, 3.7-million-square-foot, 1,200-acre development in rural Shackelford County, Texas, announced in August 2025 to meet AI demand.

San Antonio's data center growth, including Vantage's TX cluster, has concentrated on the city's West and Northwest sides where CPS Energy, the nation's largest municipally owned combined electric and gas utility, has courted large industrial and data center loads with dedicated substations and negotiated rate agreements. Bexar County and the City of San Antonio have both offered Chapter 313-successor and local property-tax abatement agreements to data center developers as part of broader economic-diversification efforts beyond the city's traditional military and tourism base. CPS Energy's long-range integrated resource planning has specifically flagged data centers as a fast-growing large-load category requiring new generation and transmission investment through the early 2030s, a dynamic Texas's ERCOT grid operator has also cited statewide as it revises long-term demand forecasts upward.

Northern Virginia's Loudoun and Prince William counties together form the largest data center market in the world by capacity, and local zoning debate has intensified in recent years as residents, county supervisors, and Dominion Energy weigh the tradeoff between substantial commercial tax revenue from facilities like this one and rising transmission-line construction, land consumption, and residential electricity-rate pressure tied to data center growth. Dominion Energy's long-range integrated resource plans have repeatedly cited Loudoun and Prince William data center demand as the single largest driver of the utility's near-term generation and transmission capital spending, a dynamic that has also drawn scrutiny from the Virginia State Corporation Commission in periodic rate cases. Vantage's Virginia cluster sits among the densest concentration of competing operators anywhere in the world, including Amazon Web Services, Equinix, Digital Realty, and QTS facilities within a few miles.

Vantage Data Centers launched in 2010 with an investment from Silver Lake Partners and is headquartered in Denver, Colorado. DigitalBridge acquired the company in March 2017, and in January 2024 Vantage announced a $6.4 billion equity investment round led by DigitalBridge and Silver Lake, with Colony Capital, AustralianSuper, GIC, and ADIA cited among its other investors.

The company operates a standardized campus model across three regions, North America, including US operations in Virginia, Arizona, California, Washington, Ohio, and Texas, plus Quebec and Montreal in Canada, EMEA, spanning Germany, Ireland, Italy, Poland, Switzerland, South Africa, and the UK, and APAC, covering Australia, Hong Kong, Japan, Malaysia, and Taiwan. Vantage's own site highlights a Texas mega-campus described as a $25 billion development with 1.4 gigawatts of capacity under development, one of the larger single-project capacity figures recorded in this registry, comparable in scale to the multi-hundred-megawatt AWS and NTT figures already documented here.

The registry here tracks 13 Vantage facilities across four states, Arizona, California, Texas, and Virginia, a subset of the six US states the operator names on its own site, which additionally lists Washington and Ohio. No aggregate global data center count or total operating MW figure, distinct from the single Texas mega-campus figure, was located in the sources reviewed this session.
